About this document


This document provides the teaching content for Te Ao Māori Years 11–13 of the
New Zealand Curriculum.

Progress and assessment information for Te Ao Māori Years 11–13 is still in
development. Once that is completed, Te Ao Māori Years 11–13 is proposed to be
made by the Minister of Education as a National Curriculum Statement under section
90(1)(a) of the Education and Training Act 2020.

It is proposed that, once made and published in the New Zealand Gazette, schools
who offer Te Ao Māori Years 11–13 will be required to start using it in Year 11 from
1 January 2028, in Year 12 from 1 January 2029, and in Year 13 from 1 January
2030.

This document will be replaced with the official version made under the Act and
published in the New Zealand Gazette once that has occurred.

  including global connections. Students will examine how historical and

Students are taught how to engage with kaupapa Māori, tikanga Māori, and
mātauranga Māori, to understand how knowledge, values, and perspectives shape
Māori understandings across historical, contemporary, and future contexts.

Te Ao Māori provides students with the knowledge and practices to examine how
knowledge is held, generated, transmitted, adapted, and applied, and how
relationships between people, place, environment, community, and tikanga influence
identity, belonging, and decision-making over time and into the future. This
disciplinary knowledge helps students to examine relationships, perspectives, and
impacts, and apply these to explain outcomes, inform decision-making, and respond
to authentic contexts and challenges.

As students progress through Years 11–13, they are taught to analyse relationships,
perspectives, continuity and change, evaluate impacts and consequences, and
explain how knowledge, values, and aspirations influence decisions and actions. This
enables them to make strategic, evidence-based insights and understanding of Te Ao
Māori that is grounded in kōrero tuku iho, mātauranga Māori, and tikanga, while
considering implications for individuals, communities, and future generations.

 Disciplinary writing: the use of writing to reflect the ways in which knowledge is organised, analysed, and communicated within the discipline.

 In Te Ao Māori, students use explicitly taught disciplinary writing to communicate, analyse, and develop understandings of Mātauranga Māori, histories, events, experiences, identities, and
 worldviews. They draw on kōrero tuku iho, culturally grounded evidence, personal and community narratives, and insights from a range of perspectives to make meaning, share knowledges, express
 ideas, and respond to issues for specific purposes and audiences.

Teaching considerations

• Emphasise the interconnected nature of whakapapa, whanaungatanga, mātauranga, tikanga, identity, belonging, and relationships with place.
• Provide opportunities for students to engage with narratives, experiences, histories, and cultural practices as sources of knowledge.
• Provide opportunities for students to investigate the impacts of historical, social, environmental, political, and cultural change.
• Explicitly teach and consistently use key Māori concepts and vocabulary across learning contexts.
• Support students to recognise how knowledge is transmitted through observation, participation, practice, storytelling, cultural expression, and relationships.
• Draw on examples that demonstrate leadership, collective responsibility, enterprise, and community participation.
• Support students to recognise that continuity can involve both maintaining and adapting knowledge, practices, and relationships.
• Facilitate discussion of tensions, trade-offs, and competing aspirations that can arise within complex issues.
• Ensure learning promotes respectful engagement with tikanga, marae contexts, and culturally significant knowledge.
